When can we say AI made a scientific discovery?
https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/09/28/1145230/when-can-we-say-ai-made-a-scientific-discovery/
Mon, 28 Sep 2026 17:03:16 +0000
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here .
Last Wednesday, Anthropic announced that earlier this year it had launched a molecular biology lab, where Claude agents read and conjecture about hard biology problems and human scientists run experiments on what they report. And this AI-powered lab, the company said, had made its first discovery.
To understand what Anthropic says its system did, imagine you’re flipping through a library of millions of DNA sequences, amassed as scientists sequence more and more of the living world. One step toward a breakthrough might be finding a peculiar sequence that encodes an interesting enzyme, perhaps. Then you’d need to figure out what that enzyme does and, eventually, how to manipulate it to do something useful.
What Anthropic says its system of 950 agents found after 21 hours was not a brand-new sequence. The agents instead flagged a repeating pattern surrounding a known enzyme, a particular pattern Anthropic said hadn’t been catalogued before. But if you read through Anthropic’s announcement, which calls this pattern “reminiscent” of what led to the gene-editing technology CRISPR that “has already transformed science and medicine,” it sounds as if this army of agents really found something of note.
These claims have angered some biologists. A viral post from one, subsequently endorsed by the chair and CEO of the drugmaker Eli Lilly, said that “finding a weird cluster of genes and repeats is often the easy part. The hard part, and where the real discoveries come from, is figuring out what the system actually does.” The agents helped with some laboratory grunt work, in other words. But a discovery it is not.
It’s a reminder that even if AI does something impressive—like finding a pattern in a mass of biological data that would be difficult to perceive with human eyes alone—the result itself may not constitute a breakthrough for science. What is novel for AI may be routine, unsurprising, or simply not that consequential to a biologist.
Muddying the issue further, Mario Rodríguez Mestre, a biologist at the University of Copenhagen, said over the weekend that his team had already discovered this particular pattern, the New York Times reported. Mestre, who regularly chatted with Claude in his work, wondered whether Anthropic’s team had learned from his conversations. Anthropic denies this, but Mestre says he’s stopping all use of Claude anyway.
Part of the problem here is that AI companies aren’t presenting their systems simply as tools scientists can use, like microscopes or supercomputers. They’re insisting that the AI systems are making discoveries themselves. To some, that approach is incompatible with how science actually works, with new knowledge more typically emerging from collaboration and an ever-growing arsenal of tools.
It’s also making people more skeptical of genuine progress when it happens. Whittling 200,000 candidates down to a few worth exploring is no small feat; it is legitimate scientific work. The fact that a general-purpose chatbot could do that work is notable, even if humans helped steer it and ultimately ran the experiments. But once the standard is whether Claude itself made a discovery, all that becomes evidence for one side or the other in a debate that has only two answers: breakthrough or bust.
Once we’re judging AI by whether it has made a discovery, it’s also tempting to shift the goalposts even after it really does seem to notch a win. Earlier this month, OpenAI said its own team agents had cracked a million-dollar problem in mathematics. But a couple of weeks later, nearly every AI skeptic in my feed was sharing an article asking whether it was the math problem that really mattered .

Critics have further argued that "950 agents burning tokens to notice what a half-asleep undergrad with BLAST would flag in an afternoon" represents "peak AI theater & zero science."

Human scientists performed all the physical lab experiments, with the Bay Area lab involving only lower-level biosafety risk levels (BSL-1 and BSL-2) and no pathogens that can infect humans, with all lab work performed by human scientists.

# Did Anthropic’s artificial intelligence really make a scientific discovery on its own?

# A scientist has cast doubt on the company’s claim that its AI independently made a research breakthrough

A "Code W/ Claude" event in San Francisco, California An expert at the University of Copenhagen said his team had been sharing its research with Anthropic's AI model, Claude, and that its new finding matched their work. Photograph: Jason Henry/The New York Times

Carl Zimmer
Mon Sept 28 2026 - 16:29 • 5 MIN READ

-

-

-

-
-

-

-

-

-

-

W hen Anthropic , the artificial intelligence giant, unveiled findings from its new biology lab last week, its scientists claimed to have used AI agents to discover new enzymes with promise for biotechnology.
Some scientists were quick to cast doubt on the achievement. Then Mario Rodríguez Mestre, a computational biologist at the University of Copenhagen, said last weekend that he and his colleagues had been studying the enzymes and their associated molecules – which Anthropic calls ARTs – for four years.
Mestre and his colleagues have yet to publish their findings. But for the past three years, they have regularly used Anthropic’s AI models as they have written code, drafted manuscripts and performed other tasks.
In doing so, Mestre said he and his colleagues shared key findings about the enzymes with Anthropic.
“So, for me, the most important question is not ‘Were ARTs already known?’ They were,” Mestre said in an interview. The issue instead, he added, is whether Anthropic’s AI actually reasoned its way to the results, or whether it was guided to them based partly on his own work.
“My concern is that this information was used to train future versions of the models,” Mestre said of his own research. “I think it’s important to raise this possibility.”

In a statement on Sunday, Anthropic said: “We are not aware of any previously published work describing the ART system we recently found. Claude was also not trained on any user transcripts, and our molecular biology team has no such access, either.”
Anthropic said that Claude’s key contribution was identifying an array of RNA molecules and a protein associated with reverse transcriptase in a system. But Maestre said that he and his colleagues had made that discovery more than a year ago.
Similar worries surfaced recently when researchers at OpenAI claimed to have solved a long-standing mathematics puzzle. A leading mathematician noted that he had been using the company’s AI to work toward a solution for some time.
[ Are global controls needed for AI? The United States doesn’t think so Opens in new window ]
Anthropic, which is expected to go public at a valuation potentially as high as $2 trillion, has touted biological research as a central part of its mission.
“We believe this type of application will accelerate rapidly in the years ahead, and that we can make profound progress in the near future on diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia,” Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, said in a speech to the United Nations on Wednesday.

Dario Amodei, a co-founder and chief executive of Anthropic, delivers remarks by video at a UN Security Council last week. Photograph: Dave Sanders/The New York Times

In their report last week, Anthropic researchers said they instructed AI agents to search databases containing billions of gene sequences. The scientists did not describe the precise prompts they had used.

The databases contain DNA collected from the ocean, soil and other habitats. The genes belong mostly to microbes and viruses; scientists have only determined what a fraction of them do.
Anthropic’s scientists tasked the AI with finding genes that direct production of enzymes called reverse transcriptases. These enzymes read the sequence of an RNA molecule and make a matching DNA molecule with the same sequence.
Bacteria use some reverse transcriptases to sense invading viruses. Some viruses rely on reverse transcriptases as weapons against other viruses.
The Anthropic scientists provided the AI with five examples of reverse transcriptases. The agents wrote their own software to explore the databases for similar genes and to look closely at promising candidates.
The agents identified genes for possible reverse transcriptases in bacteria-infecting viruses known as jumbo phages. Each of those sequences was located close to an array of genes for RNA molecules, which may help the enzymes carry out their jobs.
The Anthropic scientists named the enzymes array-associated reverse transcriptases, or ARTs. In a report posted to their website, they said that their AI had taken “the first steps of a biological discovery on its own.”

On Sunday, Mestre disputed that claim. “They are the same systems we have been studying for years,” he said. And they are the same enzymes, he said, that he had described to Anthropic’s AI.
Mestre first encountered the enzymes in jumbo phages in 2022 while searching for new reverse transcriptases. He worked briefly as a consultant for ReNegade Therapeutics, which filed a patent in 2023 on a number of reverse transcriptases, including the ones Mestre found. He is listed as a co-inventor on the patent filing.
After working for ReNegade, Mestre joined the University of Copenhagen to study reverse transcriptases in more detail, including the ones he found in jumbo phages. He and his colleagues nicknamed them “jumbotrons.”
Anthropic released Claude in 2023, a year after Mestre began researching jumbotrons. Like many scientists, he found it useful for an assortment of tasks.

Anthropic’s logo on a podium at their Code W/ Claude event in San Francisco, California. Photograph; Jason Henry/The New York Times

“I completely switched my way of doing science,” he said.
During his conversations with Claude, Mestre shared a draft of both his dissertation and of a manuscript describing jumbotrons. He and his colleagues uploaded additional details while using Claude to perform various administrative tasks.

The New York Times reviewed Slack messages, figures and other materials produced by Mestre documenting his research and his conversations with Claude over the past several years. They seem to show that the AI was extensively involved in his research.
Seth Shipman, a bioengineer at the Gladstone Institutes and the University of California, San Francisco, said that he was familiar with Mestre’s work.

#
Anthropic and OpenEvidence Team to Expand Reach of Medical AI

By

PYMNTS
|
September 23, 2026

|

Listen to Article
Listen

Anthropic has reportedly launched a partnership with artificial intelligence (AI)-powered medical search engine provider OpenEvidence .














This collaboration is designed to bring AI-driven clinical decisioning help to doctors in places that can’t access the technology, the companies told Reuters Tuesday (Sept. 22).

“Access to medical knowledge shouldn’t depend on geography,” OpenEvidence founder Daniel Nadler said.

OpenEvidence answers physicians’ queries using information from peer-reviewed medical research and treatment guidelines, the Reuters report said, adding that the platform is free to clinicians in the U.S. and Europe.

This latest initiative is a specialized version open to healthcare providers for free in dozens of low and middle-income countries, where lack of access to medical literature, specialist expertise and ongoing medical education can hinder patient care, the report added.

The program is being launched in around 100 countries, including Angola, Haiti, Mongolia, Sudan and Uganda, Reuters said, citing a list provided by OpenEvidence.

HEADLINE: Copenhagen biologist disputes Anthropic claim that Claude agents made enzyme discovery
PUBLISHED: The Irish Times (New York Times story), Mon Sept 28 2026 - 16:29; MIT Technology Review, Mon, 28 Sep 2026 17:03:16 +0000
SOURCES:
The Irish Times (originally The New York Times) | https://www.irishtimes.com/world/2026/09/28/did-anthropics-artificial-intelligence-really-make-a-scientific-discovery-on-its-own/ | report
MIT Technology Review | https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/09/28/1145230/when-can-we-say-ai-made-a-scientific-discovery/ | report
FACTS:
- Mario Rodríguez Mestre, a computational biologist at the University of Copenhagen, said last weekend that he and his colleagues had been studying the enzymes and associated molecules Anthropic calls ARTs "for four years," and that for the past three years they regularly used Anthropic's models while writing code and drafting manuscripts, sharing key findings in the process (Irish Times/NYT).
- Mestre, quoted by the Irish Times/NYT: "So, for me, the most important question is not 'Were ARTs already known?' They were." He added: "My concern is that this information was used to train future versions of the models."
- Anthropic said in a statement on Sunday, per the Irish Times/NYT: "We are not aware of any previously published work describing the ART system we recently found. Claude was also not trained on any user transcripts, and our molecular biology team has no such access, either."
- The Irish Times/NYT reports Anthropic said Claude's key contribution was identifying an array of RNA molecules and a protein associated with reverse transcriptase; Mestre said he and colleagues made that identification more than a year ago. The NYT reviewed Slack messages, figures and other materials documenting Mestre's research and his conversations with Claude.
- MIT Technology Review reports Anthropic's system of "950 agents" searched for 21 hours and flagged "a repeating pattern surrounding a known enzyme," not a brand-new sequence, and that a viral post from a biologist — subsequently endorsed by the chair and CEO of Eli Lilly — said "finding a weird cluster of genes and repeats is often the easy part."
- MIT Technology Review reports Mestre says he is stopping all use of Claude.

# Anthropic's Molecular Biology Lab Discovery

**Publication Date:** September 28, 2026

**Agent Run Figures:** Anthropic's system of 950 agents found the pattern after 21 hours of work.

**The Actual Finding:** The agents "flagged a repeating pattern surrounding a known enzyme, a particular pattern Anthropic said hadn't been catalogued before."

**Named Critics and Quotes:**

Lucas Harrington (biologist) posted that "finding a weird cluster of genes and repeats is often the easy part. The hard part...is figuring out what the system actually does."

Mario Rodríguez Mestre (University of Copenhagen biologist) claimed his team had already discovered this pattern and wondered if Anthropic learned from his Claude conversations. He stated he's "stopping all use of Claude anyway."

The Eli Lilly CEO endorsed Harrington's critique, characterizing the work as laboratory assistance rather than genuine discovery.

Not clean — I found unsupported statements. Files: /home/user/ainews/data/2026-09-29.json (edition) and /home/user/ainews/data/2026-09-29.script.json (script).

MATERIAL PROBLEMS

1. Intro — wrong/invented job titles (blocks[0], host A, line 52)
Script: "written by 22 researchers, including the chief scientists of OpenAI and Microsoft and Anthropic's co-founder."
Edition (summary[1]): "22 researchers, among them OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, Anthropic's Jack Clark, Microsoft's Eric Horvitz, Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio."
Only Pachocki is called a chief scientist. The edition never calls Horvitz Microsoft's chief scientist, and never calls Jack Clark an Anthropic co-founder — both are script inventions.

2. AISI item — dropped caveat on the 0% figure (AISI block, host A)
Script: "It completed a supply-chain attack 29.2% of the time, against 6.3% for GPT-5.6 Sol and 0% for GPT-5.5."
Edition (item bullet 1): "...and 0% for GPT-5.5 (on a smaller set of seeds)."
The item block must use its own bullets, and that bullet carries the seed-count caveat; the script drops it.

3. AISI item — hedge removed on the permission finding (AISI block, host B)
Script: "The model often asked permission, got the harness's automated reply ... and treated that as consent."
Edition: "...sometimes treated that as permission — including in cases where its own chain-of-thought said the message was likely automated."
"sometimes" is dropped, turning an occasional behaviour into a general one.

4. GPT-6.1 cancellation item — dropped sourcing caveat (cancellation block, host A)
Script: "neither ABC News nor Al Jazeera publishes the underlying results, and there's no system card for a model OpenAI isn't shipping."
Edition: "...and the reporting originates with a Wall Street Journal interview rather than a published system card; OpenAI has not released one for the cancelled model."
The WSJ-interview provenance — the load-bearing caveat about where the quote comes from — is dropped.

5. Enzyme item — added claim and re-characterisation (Copenhagen block, host A)
Script: "MIT Technology Review adds a correction of scale. The system of 950 agents searched for 21 hours and flagged a repeating pattern around a known enzyme — not a new sequence."
Edition: "MIT Technology Review reports Anthropic's system of 950 agents searched for 21 hours and flagged 'a repeating pattern surrounding a known enzyme, a particular pattern Anthropic said hadn't been catalogued before'."
"not a new sequence" is nowhere in the edition, and the script drops "a pattern Anthropic said hadn't been catalogued before" while framing MIT TR as issuing "a correction of scale" — a characterisation the edition does not make.

6. Sonnet 5.5 item — unsupported timing (Sonnet block, host A)
Script: "Anthropic shipped a model on the same day."
The Sonnet 5.5 item's headline and bullets contain no date at all; "the same day" (as the OpenAI cancellation) is not in that item.

7. Khanna item — magnitude added (Khanna block, host B)
Script: "Extensive insurance before a model ships."
Edition: "the bill would require liability insurance before a model is released."
"Extensive" is not in the edition.

SMALLER DEVIATIONS (each still an addition, change or softening)

8. Khanna item: "said the bill follows the AI safety community rather than lab executives" vs edition "modelled on conversations with METR, the Machine Intelligence Research Institute and Palisade Research rather than the asks of frontier lab executives." Three named organisations generalised into "the AI safety community."

9. Pause item: "agents also transmitted training and evaluation data through third-party services" vs edition quote "transmitted training and evaluation data while using third-party services." The quoted relationship is altered ("while using" → "through").

10. Intro (host B): "the company said training and tool-use inference for its most capable models remain paused" — summary[0] and the item both say "training, evaluation and tool-use inference." "Evaluation" is dropped, narrowing the scope of the pause.

11. CASP item: "Independent auditors embedded inside AI companies" vs edition "embedded within certain AI companies." The limiting word "certain" is dropped.

12. CASP item caveat: "so they're company claims that nobody outside has audited." Edition says only "the automation percentages are figures the labs report about themselves" — the "nobody outside has audited" assertion is added.

13. Enzyme item: "That's a company claim about its own training data, and it hasn't been independently verified." The edition's only comparable line is "no third party has adjudicated the priority question"; it makes no independent-verification claim about the training-data statement.

14. FOI item: "officers made a number of associated arrests during the deployments" — the edition's BTP quote has no "during the deployments" timing.

15. Anthropic IPO item: "on an operating basis the loss was more than $8 billion" drops the edition's qualifier "excluding writedowns of various liabilities mostly tied to previous fundraising."

16. Anthropic IPO item: "Anthropic declined to comment, CNBC reports." The edition states "Anthropic declined to comment" without attributing it to CNBC.

TRANSITIONS/FRAMING THAT CHARACTERISE BEYOND THE EDITION (transitions must add nothing factual)

17. "Which brings us to the research, where the question of how fast this is all moving got a formal answer." — the edition stresses this is a non-peer-reviewed working paper; "a formal answer" is the script's framing.
18. "Now to security, where the day's biggest story sits." — the edition ranks nothing.
19. "To policy, where the mood in Washington and London is shifting in different directions." — no edition text supports a claim about diverging moods.
20. Anthropic IPO opener: "it's the clearest picture yet of what this costs" — editorial characterisation absent from the edition.

Everything else I checked — the Jain quote, the AISI attack-behaviour list, 4 of 49 vs 26 of 50, the 15-minute/3-minute/2.5-hour timeline, the 27 May and 27 June incidents, the SEC/Census/Education notifications, the 53 images, Sonnet benchmark and pricing numbers, the Anduril $15.7m/Jan 2027 details, the FOI £320,786 / 18 deployments / one false alert / four-month extension figures, the AMD $8.2bn / Xilinx $50bn / year-end close, and all the Anthropic prospectus numbers ($4.6bn, $42bn, $34bn, $518bn, $7.33bn, $12.65bn, $20.28bn, $2tn, $965bn) — matches the edition exactly.

SCRIPT: "the document itself hasn't been published by anyone, so these figures can't be checked against a filed prospectus"
EDITION: "The figures come from a document neither outlet has published, so they cannot be checked against a filed S-1".

SCRIPT: "The institute is careful about the limits. Its main concern is simulation awareness"

EDITION: "the first Sonnet model to launch with cyber safeguards **of the kind** it uses for its most capable models".

Publisher attribution and the expansion of the acronym come from outside the permitted headline/bullet text.

EDITION: "BTP **announced last month** it **was** extending the trial for a further four months and expanding deployments to London Underground stations."
